item_title: Carrie Chapman Catt Papers: General Correspondence, circa 1890-1947; Yale Review
text:
-2-
The services of this amazing woman were far more
diversified than the work of any other leader of a settlement.
From the "cleaning up the milk" crusade to electing "reform
mayors" of Chicago, Miss Addams was in the vanguard of all
forward movements. The victories, however, were not won with-
out much bitterness which left scars behind them. Theodore
Roosevelt, it will be remembered, pronounced her Chicago's most
useful citizen and no one denied it.
Every reform or progressive law passed by the Illinois
legislature was helped along its way by the sponsorship of Miss
Addams and often by much tedious work on its behalf. Again,
the gains met hostility and left behind much resentment.
She helped the nation too. It was at Hull House that
the idea of a Children's Bureau, the first in the world, had
its birth.
The Great War must have been a severe shock to Miss
Addams. She believed devoutly in permanent peace and had written
enlightening books about it. Yet, at Hull House, official
recruiting was soon in operation and the biographer says: "All
soldiers from the district were given their last meal 'at home'
by Hull House and said their farewells in the Hull House Court-
yard." These were heartbreaking experiences, but they were help-
ing her to "think things through" again and she came to know some
truths others had not yet learned.
Always a popular lecturer, Miss Addams was now called
hither and yon to speak. Some statements she made were misquoted,
some misconstrued, and still other remarks were not in accord
with the sentiment of the people at the time. This must have
been the unhappiest period of her life. Backs were coldly turned
where approving smiles had met hers before; lost friends, con-
demnatory editorials and comments were common, and their bitterness
outdistanced those of City and State in previous periods of reform.
The news of the Ford Peace Ship, upon which she did not
go, the women's peace convention at the Hague, with its after
commissions to the war nations, were received with scant sympathy
and much scorn.
When, however, the famous "Black List" appeared with
Miss Addams' name upon it (and some hundreds of others), the
Secretary of War, Newton Baker, said: "That name lends dignity
and greatness to any list in which it appears." The war psychosis,
after a dozen years, faded away and the old popularity returned
in double measure. If an investigation should be made at some
future date into what Miss Addams really said in those somewhat
frenzied months, it doubtless would be found to be irrefutable
truth that all the world, in its sane mood, accepted.
So upon her community, her city, her state, her nation,
her world, the influence of Jane Addams fell and lingers, - an
influence based upon faith in "Peace on Earth, Good Will to Men"
and among all men and women her spirit is still marching on.
Carrie Chapman Catt

item_title: Carrie Chapman Catt Papers: General Correspondence, circa 1890-1947; Cunningham, Minnie F.
text:
Minnie Fisher Cunningham
Fisher Farms
New Waverly, Texas
August 24 1944
Dear Mrs. Catt:
Thank you so much for having sent me that biography of yourself. I have carried it with me and as time permitted I have refreshed and renewed my courage by reading about your own. From the time of the Democratic Convention in St. Louis where Ferguson presented the minority plank, which was " where I came in" I could run my own story of the South west parallel with it. It helped me to forget the heat and the crowded buses; it gave me ideas for new audacities; it was fun.
Perhaps you wonder why I needed ideas for audacities. So I will explain that in March the sister I wrote you that I was nursing died. And in April the man we had tried to get to carry the banner of decency in the gubernatorial race said he wouldn't. Our present governor is worse than Ferguson ever dared to be and has besides fought all the war agencies and defeated all the war plans that he could. The political machine under Jesse Jones and Senator O'Daniel leadership was all set to defeat the President and the governor was cooperating to the fullest.
So in May a small group of us said tha after all we were only responsible to God for what we did ourselves and not for what other people did or did not do. So I announced as candidate for governor and we made my campaign a straight, hot attack on the governor and his anti-war activities. That had the desired effect of taking his mind off the presidential election. Then we put through the bolt from the Democratic Convention where the machine operated too efficiently; and sent our delegates to Chicago.

dated New York July 7th, 1922
Miss Lutz was the official delegate appointed by the Brazilian Government to
attend the Pan American Conference of Women at the invitation of the U.S.
State Department, in Baltimore,April 1922.
Dear Mrs.Catt:-
As I take up my pen to thank you for the wonderful days spent
with you, I feel as if it were inadequate. How can I tell you what they meant
to me.
Those days of focusing of vision on questions that had
seemed blurred before;days of growth and of happiness and repose.
It seemed wonderful after having made the first steps unguided to
find in the midst of the journey,thegreat leader and to know that from now on,
Brazil is secure in her guidance and that I have found a source from which flows
all that I myself don't know and yet the others want me to teach them.
The days I spent with you were amongst the happiest not only of
those spent in this country, but in my life. Never shall I forget them in their
serenity and their peace. I shall always remember them and from that memory will
come renewed enthusiasm and strength.
I am hoping that I shall receive final instructions and then I shall
hurry home to prepare everything for the wonderful honor and great gift of your
presence among us there. Your visit to Brazil will be for us the greatest gift
Brazilian women ever had. With deep and most heartfelt thanks,
Yours ever
Bertha Lutz

Mrs. William Tilton,

My dear Mrs. Tilton,
I am laid up in bed with a broken leg and one of the things I have done has been to make a firm determination that I will connect myself with no further obligations. I have some left from the old schedule and to which I must still adhere. I will not take on any new ones, so I am not going to join your Committee. It would mean letters to be answered and appeals to be made. I am too tired and not well enough to take these things on. You must excuse me. Folks do get old and worn out if you give them time enough. I am sorry that I cannot keep on forever.
Sincerely yours,
Carrie Chapman Catt

Dear Mrs. Griffing,
Mrs. Hooker makes the proposition to take the entire
responsibility of the Washington meeting. I gave her my consent very
willingly. I suppose she will write to you, if so, do say yes. She
thinks she could manage the cause more discreetly, more genteelly than

I am speaking every night to fine audience, sometimes
on suffrage, sometimes on marriage and divorce. I shall be a resevoir

To Elizabeth Smith Miller from Mrs. Stanton
Johnstown, N.Y. September 18, 1871
Dear Liz,
Mama died last Friday and yesterday we laid her in the bosom
of old mother earth, a pleasant sunshiny day, everything looking green
and beautiful, Her death was a calm and peaceful sleep, nothing more,
it was scarcely perceptible when she passed away. She sat up in
easy chair a few hours before she died and ate her breakfast as usual.
She soon complained of feeling very drowsy and laid down to her last
sweet sleep.
I was very glad that I had returned in time from California
to spend two days here a week ago. Mama was so very impatient to see me.
Lovingly,
E. C. S.

choice lay between that and nothing.
Ever yours,
E. C. S.

In 1951, in her 88th year, Dr. Terrell was one of those who brought
the Test Case challenging the validity of the 1872 and 1873 Civil Rights
statutes, which eventually resulted in the opening of Washington restaurants
to all regardless of race.
In 1953, Dr. Terrell again made headlines when she defied the segregation
rule in the Washington theatres, and successfully initiated activities
to end these practices; for today, Washington theatres are open to all.
Only a few weeks ago she was one of a group of citizens to go to
Georgia and petition Gov. Talmadge to release Mrs. Ingram.
It is small wonder that the editor of the Washington Post said of her
and I quote "Hers' has been a long record of conquests--Washington has been
enriched by her presence here."
May I add that not only Washington, but the whole human race has been
enriched by touching shoulders with her. She has truly been a builder of
bridges for the youth who follow after her.
In closing may I say that the Philadelphia Cotillion Society is to be
congratulated on having chosen so worthy an individual on whom to bestow
the much coveted diamond Cross of Malta, and to have done it while she
may still know that her life work has not been in vain and is appreciated.
May God bless you, Mrs. Terrell, and spare you to us for many more

This was written for the Delta Sigma Theta Sorority of which she is an

1. I will strive to reach the highest educational, moral and
spiritual efficiency which I can possibly attain.
2. I will never lower my aims for any temporary benefit which
might be gained.
3. I will endeavor to preserve my health, for however great
one's mental and moral strength may be, physical weakness
prevents the accomplishments of much that might otherwise
be done.
4. I will close my ears and seal my lips to slanderous gossip.
5. I will labor to ennoble the ideals and purify the atmosphere

7. I will take an active interest in the welfare of my country,
using my influence toward the enactment of laws for the
protection of the unfortunate and weak and for the repeal

rights.
8. I will never belittle my race, but encourage all to hold it
in honor and esteem.
9. I will not shrink from undertaking what seems to be wise and
good, because I labor under the double handicap of race and
sex, but striving to preserve a calm mind with a courageous
cheerful spirit, barring bitterness from my heart, I will

THE REVIVAL SEASON
With the opening of the new year
comes the season of religious revivals,
in which many of the churches unite
to dispel the indifference that routine
begets in the most faithful members as
well as to gather into the folds those
who are still walking in religious darkness.
Of the propriety and utility of
revivals as an aid to the permanent
growth of the chruch, there are two
opinions. Many pastors feel that they
are necessary in order to get the churches
out of a religious [?] and to arouse
concerted efforts against the growing
forces of evil in the community.
To achieve this end special efforts are
made to combine in holding religious
services, conducted by some noted evangelist
who preaches every night for a
week or longer, aided by gifted gospel
singers and a choir augmented by the
union of many churches. Nothing is
omitted that will add to the emotional
and spectacular effect and many are
drawn to attend these meetings for this
reason. With an attendance of many
hundreds, or even thousands assured,
the task of the evangelist is to arouse the
emotional side of his hearers until they
evince a renunciation of evil and avow
a desire to become converted to better
things. This change of heart, as it is
sometimes styled, may be accompanied
by much noise and physical demonstrations,
the degree of ardor manifested being
taken to denote the spiritual conflict
involved. How permanent the conversions
are that result from these revivals
it is hard to tell.

item_title: Mary Church Terrell Papers: Subject File, 1884-1962; National American Woman Suffrage Association, proceedings and reports; 1893-1905, undated
text:
PREFACE
______
Since the union of the National and the American
Woman Suffrage Associations there has been no
pamphlet report of the annual convention until now.
The work of preparing this report was placed in the
hands of the Press Committee of '92, with instructions
to engage a stenographer, to condense State reports,
and to omit the publication of evening speeches.
The delay in issuing the pamphlet was due to the fact
that nearly every page had to be verified. The committee
wished to make this hand-book of the
Association for the year; with all committees in full,
all lists in alphabetical order, all names properly
spelled, and addresses correctly given. The delegates
and officers had been so unaccustomed to preparing
their reports for printing that names were illegible,
figures were indistinct, and pages unnumbered. Committees
were dilatory in submitting their financial reports.
Many of the State reports were not officially
signed. Numbers of regularly elected delegates did
not deem it necessary to bring with them regularly
signed credentials, but filled out with pencil new
credentials at the convention; in some case giving
only their surname. States were late in sending in
dues, and we go to press with one State uncertain as to
correctness.
None of these shortcomings are referred to in order
to chide the shortcomer, but to show that all the errors
in this report can not be laid at the door of the Press
Committee. Another year, we will all have profited by
our experiences.
The committee is greatly indebted to Miss Anthony,
whose advice was invaluable and whose longer experience
and acquaintance with the work and the workers,
enabled many corrections to be made which could not
have been made without her help. The convention
numbers of the Woman's Tribune and the Woman's
Journal were of great assistance. The editors and the
committee worked together to make both papers and
the pamphlet contain matter of interest to suffragists.
The committee is aware of some irregularities in the
report; for instance, the memorial speeches were
neither discussions not reports of committees, and
were not therefore, under the rules established, properly
publishable. Yet here were our veteran workers
telling us of the deeds of their departed associates,
explaining their sacrifices and depicting their strong
characters, and it seemed but duty to preserve such
history.
During the time (six weeks) which it has taken to
prepare this book, the committee has tried to keep in
mind the interest of the Association, and it believes
that the spirit of gentleness and justice which existed
among the delegates and members of the Twenty-fifth
Annual Convention will be found with the readers of
this report.
Harriet Taylor Upton,
Chairman Press Committee N.A.W.S.A. for 1892.

A SHORT BIOGRAPHY OF CHRISTIAN ABRAHAM FLEETWOOD
Christian Fleetwood was born in Baltimore, Maryland, July 21,
1840, to Charles and Ann Maria Fleetwood, both free people of
color. His father was employed as head steward in the household
of the John C. Brunes, wealthy aristocrats active in the sugar
trade, Mr. Brune being a Merchant "Prince".
Young Fleetwood's education began at the hands of Mrs. Brune,
in the Brune home, when the lad was about four or five years old.
We learn how this circumstance, odd for Baltimore in the eighteen-forties,
came about from a sketch in the Washington Bee (April 11,
1885). It was written by one of Fleetwood's senior contemporaries,
William E. Matthews, who had also contributed to the Lyceum
Observer prior to Fleetwood's abandonment of this venture (which
he with several of his associates started about 1860) to volunteer
on the Union side in the Civil war of the rebellion among the
states. Excerpts from this sketch are quoted below.
"Our first recollection of young Fleetwood was the novel
sight of seeing him a child of four or five years, elegantly
dressed in embroidered jacket and silken hose, the pet and
pride of the household, sitting with Mrs. Brune at the parlour

parents in the neighborhood .... Mrs. Brune, who was
childless, took a great fancy to the boy and treated him almost

With treaties frankly expressed and honorably ratified renouncing war, war between the European and American nations would in a generation
or so become a discarded habit.
Not so in the Pacific and the fields of economic exploitation. Economic conferences should and probably will solve the problems of
rivalry between nations for markets. Probably open doors and free chances for all will be the solution.
Imagine John Doe, American, rich, energetic and ambitious.
Kingships and kingdoms are no longer fashionable and banditry on a grand scale no longer offers adventure; so he decides to build a world
rubber trust as the most inviting road to power. At the same moment,
Richard Roe, British, equally rich and vaccuous as to a life work, conceives
the same aim; and each starts in a different dependency of his respective country and in time each achieves a monopoly and then discovers
the other impertinently blocking his path[.]to world control.
Like Alexanders or [and] Napoleons they pit themselves against each other.
Meanwhile we, the suppliant people of these respective lands, having been taxed to maintain a great navy with its accompaniment of marines,
airplanes, bombs, poison gas, etc, etc, in order to be ready, now come
forward with banners flying to back our particular magnate, under the
usual cry of "protection to life and property." The example is far
less fatuous than it sounds. If there is another war it will be quite
as sordid but not so simple as this example.
My solution of the disarmament question is to proceed by a flank movement to build up a peace institution that will be position and aggressive, not negative; compacts that will employ the word SHALL, not
may; put the peace institution under the State Department and develop

that Department into an active power for peace. Let the new peace institution be endowed with some of the eighty-two cents per dollar now going to the war institution and give the State Department a publicity
section through which to educate the public on the principles involved in the changing status of peace vs. war, and give to it money with which to provide speakers and writers to defend its policies.
Keep the building going until confidence in the positive aggressiveness of peace produces in all the advanced countries the sense of security, as it certainly will. Disarmament will follow as quietly as barnacles drop off a ship in fresh waters. Why have armaments
when war has gone out of fashion? You may say the abolition of
war is an impossible ideal. It is as certain to come as the sun is
sure to rise to-morrow.
